summary.text:
Cheshire East's Treasury Management Strategy went to Audit and Governance Committee on 20 March 2026 as a five-page covering report noting-and-commenting on the strategy already approved by Council on 25 February 2026 inside the MTFS 2026-2030. All treasury figures live in Appendix 1 (Annex 7 of the MTFS, doc 131505); the covering report itself carries no numbers and is titled "Treasury Management Strategy Decision Report Template (delete as appropriate)" — a drafting placeholder not cleaned up before publication.

Position at 31 December 2025: £376m of gross external debt, of which Local Authorities £187m at 4.43%, PWLB Fixed £144m at 4.68%, LOBOs £12m at 4.50% and Other £13m at 3.98% (blended 4.58%), plus £19m PFI and £1m of leases as other long-term liabilities. Treasury investments £45m (blended 4.57%) split between £25m in-house instant-access money at 3.89% and £20m in externally-managed pooled funds spanning property, multi-asset, equity, global income and corporate bond mandates. Net debt £331m. Adviser Arlingclose, contract running to 31 December 2026.

Balance-sheet identity closes in every column of Table 1 (Appendix 1 p.5). At 31/03/26 CFR £539.392m − external borrowing £283.888m − OLTL £16.638m = internal borrowing £238.866m exactly; the identity holds at 31/03/27, /28, /29 and /30. What Table 1 then shows is a one-year restructuring of striking size: internal borrowing jumps from £238.866m to £446.123m between 31 March 2026 and 31 March 2027 — around £207m of the balance sheet moving from external debt to the Authority's own cash inside twelve months — and thereafter sits at 78%-82% of Loans CFR through to 2029/30. §7.26 makes the reasoning explicit: short rates are expected to fall further and internal resources / short-term borrowing are seen as more cost-effective than fixing long. The liability benchmark (Table 2, p.6) rises to £479.197m by 31/03/27 then declines, leaving a gap to Loans CFR that widens from £94.421m at 31/03/26 to £119.580m by 31/03/30.

The forecast the internal-borrowing bet is priced against sits in Annex A (p.18). Arlingclose's central case has Bank Rate at 3.25% by June 2026 and held at 3.25% out to December 2028, with 5-year gilt at 3.80% and 20-year at 4.95% at the same date. Six months on the market has answered it: Bank Rate remains 3.75%, OIS 1Y 4.11%, and the long end of the PWLB certainty curve — 5-year 5.34%, 10-year 5.83%, 25-year 6.46%, 50-year 6.27% at 2026-08-14 (notice 314/26 PM) — sits about half to three-quarters of a point above where Annex A's "current" column was recorded. The 3.75% short-term new-borrowing assumption at §7.17 is still in reach because Bank Rate hasn't moved from the starting point; what has moved is the fall Arlingclose was expecting to have happened by now.

LOBOs (§7.33) fit the sector-wide refusal pattern the library is now tracking: £12m held, all with options during 2026/27, one loan already repaid, and the Authority stating explicitly it will take the option to repay if lenders exercise. Cheshire East would be the 13th council in the library to refuse a call if it happens.

Loan-book reconciliation does not tie. Paper's Annex B PWLB Fixed £144m at 4.68% at 31/12/2025 sits against our as-at snapshot of 37 loans totalling £125.6m at 4.6496% — £18.4m short and 3bp below on rate. Same ledger shows zero loans at 2024-03-31 and 2025-03-31 but 37 at 2025-12-31, suggesting the file loses pre-2025 loans keyed to this borrower name. Data-quality issue on our side, recorded in facts.loan_file_reconciliation and kept out of the email per PIPELINE guidance.

What is not raised externally: our loan-book reconciliation gap; the §7.20 EFS reference (their sentence, not ours to reopen); the asymmetric interest-rate limit; the adviser retender window; the covering-report title placeholder; and the .go.uk typo in the contact-officer email address on covering-report p.5 (actual domain is cheshireeast.gov.uk). S151 of record is Ashley Hughes, Executive Director of Resources — named in the report author line and §9. Contact Officer Chris Benham, Director of Finance — the only email address published on the paper. Primary send address chris.benham@cheshireeast.gov.uk (correcting the printed .go.uk truncation).

officer.body:
Dear Chris,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. More — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — is in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep both of those relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. A couple of thoughts below on the Treasury Management Strategy that went to Audit and Governance on 20 March — Council had already approved it inside the MTFS 2026-2030 on 25 February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The strategy is clearly laid out and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

The clearest thing on your Table 1 (Appendix 1, page 5) is what changes in a single year. Internal borrowing rises from £238.866m at 31 March 2026 to £446.123m the year after — around £207m of the balance sheet shifting from external debt to your own cash inside twelve months, and thereafter sitting between 78% and 82% of Loans CFR through to 2029/30. Paragraph 7.26 makes the reasoning explicit — short rates are expected to fall further, so internal resources and short-term loans are seen as more cost-effective than fixing long. A striking shape of restructuring; the swing itself is roughly the size of a mid-sized council's entire external book.

Which turns to the forecast the bet is priced against. Annex A (page 18) has Bank Rate at 3.25% by June 2026 and held there out to December 2028, with 5-year gilt at 3.80% at the same date. Six months on the market has answered differently: Bank Rate remains 3.75%, the OIS 1-year is around 4.11%, and yesterday afternoon's PWLB certainty curve was 5-year 5.34%, 10-year 5.83%, 25-year 6.46%, 50-year 6.27% — the long end about half to three-quarters of a point above where Annex A's "current" column was set. Your 3.75% short-term assumption at 7.17 is still in reach because Bank Rate hasn't moved from your starting point; what has moved is the fall Arlingclose was expecting to have happened by now.

The LOBO position at 7.33 fits a pattern we've been watching build across our library. You hold £12m, all with options during 2026/27, and the strategy is explicit that if lenders exercise you'll take the option to repay. Twelve councils we've read this year have refused calls that way — Wolverhampton three of them, Bath and NE Somerset's two KBC loans going floating on six-monthly resets, Dexia calling at Kent and Tameside in the same window, most recently Harrow and Staffordshire. Nobody in the twelve has accepted a rate revision. Not a surprise given today's curve, but the sector-wide picture is one nobody publishes and only builds by joining papers up.

We price every published PWLB book daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. Note our own file for Cheshire East doesn't currently tie to your Annex B — a data-quality issue on our side we're working on — so we're not going to quote our aggregates against yours today. Indicative only in any case; only the DMO can quote a binding settlement.

One standing point because CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151: the liability benchmark pathway becomes central, with an interactive version at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. On your numbers the gap between Loans CFR and the benchmark widens from around £94m at 31 March 2026 to £120m by 31 March 2030, so the useful view is probably the shape of that widening against the mix of internal balances and short-term borrowing that has to fund it.

On training, three courses fit the paper. Balance sheet projections covers what Table 1 is doing. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice picks up the widening gap. LOBO loans (legacy) sits behind the 7.33 decision. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if any of it's useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Management Strategy Report to Audit and Governance Committee, 20 March 2026, at http://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s131504/treasury-management-strategy-decision-report-template-delete.pdf, with Appendix 1 at http://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s131505/appendix-1-for-treasury-management-strat.pdf.
